title: Use non-verbal communication in extension and development

lessons.title: Elements of non-verbal communication
lessons.html:
Communication without words

Much of what people understand in a conversation comes not from the words but from how they are delivered and from what the body shows. In extension, farmers judge your sincerity, respect and competence partly through non-verbal signals long before they evaluate your technical advice. Non-verbal communication also includes visual aids and demonstrations that carry meaning without spoken language.

Main channels of non-verbal communication

ChannelExamples in extension
Body language and postureStanding with arms folded, leaning in while listening, sitting at the same level as farmers
Facial expressionSmiling in greeting, showing concern when a farmer describes stock losses
Eye contactDirect, lowered or avoided, with meanings that differ between cultures
GesturesPointing, beckoning, hand signs for numbers or approval
TouchHandshakes, including the three-part African handshake, and touching an animal during a demonstration
Space and positioningDistance between people, where the extensionist stands in a group
Voice qualitiesTone, volume, pace, pauses
Appearance and objectsClothing, the official vehicle, a laptop or clipboard
TimePunctuality, patience, how long you stay after the meeting

Functions of non-verbal signals

  • Reinforcing: nodding while saying yes.
  • Contradicting: saying you have time while checking your watch, which undermines trust.
  • Substituting: a thumbs-up instead of words.
  • Regulating: a raised hand to signal a turn to speak.
  • Expressing emotion and attitude: respect, impatience, interest or boredom.

When verbal and non-verbal messages contradict each other, listeners tend to believe the non-verbal message. Professional practice therefore requires awareness and deliberate management of one's own non-verbal behaviour.

lessons.title: Culture, context and reading non-verbal cues
lessons.html:
Non-verbal meaning depends on culture

The same signal can mean different things in different South African communities. An extensionist working across cultures must interpret carefully and avoid quick judgements.

Examples of cultural variation

  • Eye contact: in many traditional African settings, a younger person or a person of lower status lowers the eyes when speaking to an elder as a sign of respect. An extensionist who reads this as dishonesty or lack of interest misunderstands the situation. Equally, staring directly at an elder may appear disrespectful.
  • Greetings: a proper greeting may include a handshake held for some time, a slight bow or receiving with both hands. Rushing the greeting signals disrespect.
  • Sitting and standing: in some communities it is respectful to sit when an elder sits, or not to stand over seated elders. Women may sit separately at a meeting.
  • Dress: very formal clothing may create distance with farmers in the field, while very casual dress may seem disrespectful at a meeting with a traditional council.
  • Silence: pauses may signal thinking, disagreement or respect, rather than lack of understanding.

Reading cues from clients

Observe clusters of signals rather than a single one, and consider the context. A farmer with folded arms may be cold, not defensive. Signs that farmers may disagree or not understand include polite agreement with no questions, side glances among group members, restless movement or people leaving early. Respond by checking understanding in a non-threatening way: ask a farmer to demonstrate the step, or ask what problems they foresee in applying it.

Power and status signals

Official vehicles, uniforms, standing at the front with a laptop and speaking from a raised position can signal authority and distance. In participatory work, reduce these signals: park away from the meeting, sit in the circle, use the ground or a flip chart that participants can also draw on, and let farmers handle materials.

Self-awareness

Ask a trusted colleague to observe you during a session and give feedback on your posture, eye contact, voice and use of space. Small adjustments often produce large improvements in rapport.

lessons.title: Using visual and demonstration methods
lessons.html:
Showing instead of telling

Non-verbal methods are especially powerful where literacy levels vary, where several languages are spoken, or where a practical skill must be learned.

Method and result demonstrations

  • Method demonstrations show how to do something step by step: calibrating a knapsack sprayer, body condition scoring of cattle, setting a drip line, making a trench bed. Perform each step slowly, let participants watch from where they can see clearly, then let them practise while you observe.
  • Result demonstrations show the effect of a practice, such as side-by-side plots with and without lime, or a well-managed camp beside an overgrazed one. The visible difference communicates more than any lecture.

Where demonstrations involve hazards, such as chemicals, livestock handling or machinery, model correct safety behaviour visibly: wear the protective equipment, use the crush pen, keep observers at a safe distance. Participants copy what they see you do.

Visual aids

  • Pictures, posters and photo sequences with few words.
  • Real objects: healthy and diseased leaves, ticks in a jar, seed samples, a weighband.
  • Participatory maps and diagrams drawn with stones, sticks and seeds on the ground.
  • Colour coding, such as traffic-light charts for veld condition or stock health.
  • Short videos on a phone or projector, ideally showing local farmers.

Designing effective visuals

  1. Pre-test pictures with a few community members to make sure they are understood as intended.
  2. Use local settings, people, animals and crops so learners recognise them.
  3. Keep one message per picture.
  4. Be careful with symbols that may have different meanings, such as arrows, crosses or colours.

Evaluating your non-verbal communication

Check whether the message arrived: observe participants practising, ask them to explain a picture back to you, and follow up on farms to see whether the practice is applied correctly.

Key points

  • Non-verbal signals include body language, eye contact, gestures, space, voice, appearance and time.
  • When words and body language conflict, people tend to believe the body language.
  • Interpret signals in their cultural context and avoid quick judgements.
  • Reduce status signals in participatory work.
  • Use demonstrations and pre-tested visuals, and model safe behaviour.
